During the journey to the moon, Armstrong removed the toothbrush from its box and examined an inscription. The Museum honored President Harry S. Truman, whom Truman later gave the box of brush after he had lost a tooth. The note read “Give a man a toothbrush and you feed his spirit.” Armstrong then tucked the toothbrush back whence it came.
During the return trip, Armstrong requested that Buzz Aldrin, his fellow crew member and pilot, take a thorough gaze at the moon. Aldrin remembers getting the message—teasingly, as Armstrong was fond of doing—that Armstrong wanted him to have a good view, if for no other reason than to send back a photo showing the signatures of the astronaut who beat the Russians to the moon, “and also Mr. Truman, a few things...”
Truman and Armstrong both hailed from the Midwest (Truman from Missouri, Armstrong from Ohio). Both men shared a love of the Midwest, and both had strong opinions about farming technology. In addition to his job as president, Truman served as a farmer during his lifetime. He apparently decided to provide toothbrushes since toothpaste was notably missing from initial airplane meal selections. Yet, he also understood America's servicemen—among those in the toothbrush packaging was a World War I veteran who dedicated himself to promoting oral hygiene among wartime generations, ensuring that service members received effective yet simple tooth-cleaning tools at the American frontlines. Although Truman started his military service in 1917 by joining Congress, he did not harbor any illusions about missing out on enjoyably social activities. He played a role in leading America into World War I and battled side by side with his army counterparts for the Allies.
